video_title: If You Want Peace, Prepare for War
gist: Joe Lonsdale interviews Reagan Institute director Roger Zakheim about his book Peace Through Strength, on how Reagan's sustained ~$2 trillion, 5-6%-of-GDP military buildup (and SDI) won the Cold War without firing a shot. They draw lessons for competing with China today: a hollowed-out industrial base, neo-primes like Anduril, Palantir and Saronic-style autonomous boats displacing legacy primes, and cheap mass-produced munitions replacing 1980s platforms.

insights.claim: Defense-tech 'neo primes' such as Palantir, Anduril and SpaceX went from being treated with hostility by the primes and the DoD to being the most sought-after companies at the Reagan National Defense Forum; legacy primes now actively want to partner with them.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Partnership demand from incumbents validates neo-prime business models; watch prime/neo-prime teaming deals as a signal of share shift.
insights.quote: the primes in particular want a partner

insights.claim: Joe Lonsdale's 10-year view is that the best-run new defense companies will eventually take over and the legacy primes will be split up and absorbed into them.
insights.speaker: Joe Lonsdale
insights.so_what: Contrarian long-horizon bet against incumbent primes in favor of venture-backed defense tech; frames a consolidation/M&A thesis.
insights.quote: I think eventually the best run companies that are the new companies will probably take over and the primes will be split up and put into them.

insights.claim: A Secretary of the Air Force once questioned why he had to sit with Anduril at the Defense Forum; years later the Air Force is partnering with such firms because its future is seen to rely on autonomy and AI integration.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Shows how fast institutional buyer sentiment toward autonomy flipped; autonomy is now mainstream procurement territory.

insights.claim: Raytheon produces only about 60 to 80 Tomahawk missiles per year, while a startup Lonsdale knows is testing equivalent systems at less than a fifth of the cost and plans to make thousands next year.
insights.speaker: Joe Lonsdale
insights.so_what: Cost-curve disruption of munitions (5x cheaper, 10x+ volume) threatens prime pricing power in precision strike; watch low-cost cruise-missile entrants.
insights.quote: Raytheon makes like 60 to 80 Tomahawk missiles right now a year

insights.claim: Saronic-type autonomous boats are cited as a standout defense-tech story from Operation Epic Fury, with 180-foot autonomous vessels already rolling off the line in Austin and operating in the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim / Joe Lonsdale
insights.so_what: Autonomous maritime platforms are moving from prototype to production and combat use; a key neo-prime category for Navy budgets.
insights.quote: We got a few of the 180 footers already rolling off the line.

themes.theme: Industrial base and rebuild for China

insights.claim: China (the PLA) is undertaking the largest military modernization since the Soviet Union, making today's challenge more significant than understood 13 years ago.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Structural tailwind for sustained US defense spending growth.
insights.quote: that's the largest military modernization we've seen since the Soviet Union

insights.claim: Unlike Reagan, who inherited idle Vietnam-era industrial capacity that could quickly absorb new capital, the US today lacks that surge capacity because the Clinton-era consolidation left only just-in-time manufacturing for a limited set of platforms.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Capital alone won't buy output quickly; manufacturing capacity (new factories, new production methods) is the bottleneck and investable layer.
insights.quote: they effectively consolidated the industrial base to the point that we only had just in time manufacturing

insights.claim: China's industrial base is in some ways ahead of the US, though Lonsdale believes the US remains better at innovation, so the US must win with better technology and concepts of operations rather than quantity.
insights.speaker: Joe Lonsdale / Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Favors firms offering qualitative/technological edge and new manufacturing approaches over mass legacy production.

insights.claim: Because the US will be rebuilding, it will not reuse 1980s manufacturing systems; Zakheim sees the need to reconceive how defense goods are manufactured, with technology, AI and autonomy as core contributors.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Supports advanced-manufacturing and autonomy plays inside the defense supply chain.

insights.claim: Many 1980s platforms (Patriot, Apache, Abrams, Bradley, B-1/B-2, F-15/F-16/F-18, Tomahawk, a 600-ship navy) remain the backbone of the US military and are only now being replaced 40-50 years later because they have become old and expensive.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim / Joe Lonsdale
insights.so_what: A large legacy-platform recapitalization cycle is beginning, creating replacement demand that new entrants can compete for.
insights.quote: All the things were finally replacing 40, 50 years later because they've gotten old and expensive.

insights.claim: Reagan raised defense spending 20%+ in his first year and sustained it year over year for roughly $2 trillion over eight years, taking defense from about 3-4% of GDP under Carter to a 5-6% range at the peak (over 6% at one point).
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Historical benchmark for what a true buildup looks like; compare current defense/GDP ratios to gauge how much budget upside a China-driven buildup could bring.
insights.quote: 20 plus percent the first year, consistently year over year, $2 trillion over eight years

insights.claim: Sustained, multi-year investment is what made the buildup work: Reagan resisted repeated cut attempts from his OMB director David Stockman, Democrats, Republican senators, and even after the 1987 Black Monday crash.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Defense budget durability depends on political commitment through deficits and market shocks; watch whether leadership protects defense growth during fiscal stress.

insights.claim: Roughly a third of Reagan's ~3,000 public statements as president were about the military buildup, meaning he made the case to the public about every three days.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Sustained presidential messaging is a leading indicator of durable defense appropriations.
insights.quote: Just shy of a third of his public statements were about the build up.

insights.claim: The Weinberger approach was to keep existing platforms and retire legacy systems only once the modernized replacement was ready, never trading today's capability for a promised future one — an approach only possible with sufficient capital.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Under ample budgets, expect legacy sustainment revenue to persist alongside new programs rather than abrupt divestitures.

insights.claim: Zakheim rejects the 'continuity thesis' that Reagan merely continued Carter: Carter was anti-defense, though Harold Brown's lab investments matured in 1981-84 and needed Reagan's capital infusion to move 'from the lab to the field' and into scaled production.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Lab-stage tech needs a large production-funding push to matter; the scaling phase is where defense value is created.
insights.quote: We need to move this from the lab to the field.

insights.claim: The F-117 stealth fighter from Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works, cultivated during the Reagan buildup, penetrated Iraq's sophisticated air defenses in Gulf War I with none shot down, enabling air superiority.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Illustrates the long-dated payoff of breakthrough defense R&D.

themes.theme: Missile defense from SDI to Golden Dome

insights.claim: SDI was the most consequential defense program of Reagan's presidency and had the biggest impact on winning the Cold War; Golden Dome owes its lineage to what Reagan contemplated.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Space-based/strategic missile defense has strong ideological and historical backing; supports long-run Golden Dome funding.
insights.quote: It was the most consequential defense program in Reagan's presidency

insights.claim: SDI was conceived as unleashing the American entrepreneurial spirit rather than merely a military platform, and Gorbachev knew the Soviets could never compete with that.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Technology competition can impose unaffordable costs on rivals; supports funding frontier defense tech vs. China.
insights.quote: For Reagan, it was unleashing the American entrepreneurial spirit.

insights.claim: Gorbachev discovered Soviet defense spending was about 40% of the economy (he had been told under 10%), yet the USSR still trailed the US; SDI plus Chernobyl helped crack the Soviet Union.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Shows how arms races can exhaust a less productive economy; relevant to assessing China's sustainable defense burden.

insights.claim: Missile defenses used by Israel and in Operations Epic Fury and Midnight Hammer would not exist without Reagan's early commitment to missile defense despite immature technology at the time — analogous to venture capital seeding ideas that later pay off.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Patient funding of immature defense tech yields large later payoffs; supports long-duration missile-defense investment.

insights.claim: Lonsdale argues the US can no more trust China not to pursue certain AI research under an agreement than it could trust the Soviets to give up nuclear weapons, because closed societies can break agreements without whistleblowers.
insights.speaker: Joe Lonsdale
insights.so_what: Expect skepticism toward AI arms-control deals and continued US push in AI competition rather than restraint.
insights.quote: you could trust China today not to do certain AI research if we make a bigger agreement. You obviously cannot

insights.claim: At Reykjavik Reagan refused to give up SDI even in exchange for eliminating nuclear weapons, embodying 'trust but verify' and negotiating from strength.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim
insights.so_what: Strategic-tech programs tend to be protected in negotiations; low risk of being bargained away.

insights.claim: Reagan gave the military roughly a 24% pay raise in his first year and refused to reinstate the draft, which restored recruitment and pride in the all-volunteer force; Lonsdale says troops probably need better pay today too.
insights.speaker: Roger Zakheim / Joe Lonsdale
insights.so_what: Personnel cost increases are a recurring budget claimant that can compete with procurement dollars.
insights.quote: He gave them a 24% raise roughly in the first year.
